source_text: Verum quoniam de tantis et talibus rebus disserentibus non suffieit humanis sensibus et communi intellectui summam rei committere et, ut ita dixerim, visibiliter de invisibilibus pronuntiare, assumenda sunt nobis ad probationem horum, quae dicimus, etiam divinarum scripturarum testimonia. Quae testimonia ut certam et indubitatam "tree d o habeant fidem sive in his, quae dicenda a nobis, sive quae iam dicta sunt, necessarium prius videtur ostendere quod ipsae scripturae divinae sint, id est dei spiritu inspiratae. lgitur quam poterimus breviter etiam de hoc adsignabimus ex ipsis divinis scripturis quae nos conpetenter moverint proferentes, id est de Moyseo primo, legislatore gentis Hebraeae, et ex verbis lesu Christi, auctoris et principis Christianorum religionis et dogmatis. Cum enim permulti legislatores extiterint apud Graecos et barbaros, innumeri quoque doctores vel philosophi veritatem se pollicentes adserere, nullum meminimus legislatorem adfectum quendam et studium etiam exterarum gentium animis inicere potuisse, ut leges suas vel susciperent libenter vel cum omni animi intentione defenderent. Nemo ergo eam quae sibi visa est veritatem non solum pluribus aliis exteris nationibus, ‚sed ne uni quidem genti ita insinuare atque inolescere potuit, ut ad omnes eius scientia vel credulitas perveniret. Et quidem dubitari non potest quod et legislatores optaverint observari ab omnibus, si fieri posset, hominibus leges suas, et magistri, omnibus innotescere eam quae sibi visa fuerat veritatem. Sed scientes quia id omnino non possent, nee virtus in eis aliqua tanta subsisteret, quae etiam exteras nationes ad legum suarum vel adsertionum observantiam provocaret, ne conari quidem hoc aut incipere omnino ausi sunt, ne inprudentes eos etiam in hoc inefficax et inexplebile notaret inceptum. At vero in omni orbe terrarum, in omni Graecia atque universis exteris nationibus innumeri sunt et inmensi, qui relictis patris legibus et his, quos putabant deos, ad observantiam Moysi legis et discipulatum se Christi ceultumque tradiderunt, et hoc non sine ingenti odio adversum se commoto eorum, qui simulacra venerantur, ita ut ab his frequenter et cruciatibus adfligantur, nonnumquam etiam agantur in mortem; amplectuntur tamen et cum omni affectu custodiunt doctrinae Christi sermonem. Et est videre quomodo brevi tempore ipsa religio creverit, poenis eultorum mortibusque proficiens, sed et bonorum direptionibus atque omni ab his suppliciorum genere tolerato; et eo maxime mirum est quod ne doctores quidem ipsi vel satis idonei sunt vel satis plures: “praedicatur’ tamen sermo iste -in omni orbe terrarum”, ita ut ‘Graeci ac barbari, sapientes et insipientes’ religionem Christianae doctrinae suscipiant. Ex quo dubium non est “non haec humanis’ viribus aut ‘opibus” agi, ut cum omni potestate et creduhtate sermo Christi lesu apud omnium mentes atque animos convalescat. Nam et praedicta esse ab eo haec ipsa et divinis ab eo responsis confirmata, manifestum est cum dicit quia “apud praesides et iudices adducemini propter me, in testimonium ipsis et gentibuse; et rursum: “Praedieabitur hoe evangelium in omnibus gentibus”; et iterum: “Multi mihi dicent in illa die: Domine, domine, nonne in tuo nomine mandueavimus et bibimus, et in tuo nomine daemonia eiecimus? et dicam eis: Discedite a me, operarii iniquitatis s numquam cognovi vosc”. Quae si ita quidem dicta ab eo fuissent nee tamen ad finem ea, quae praedicta sunt, pervenissent, fortassis minus esse vera viderentur nec habere aliquid auctoritatis. Nune vero cum in effectum res, quae fuerant ab eo praedictae, perveniant, cum tanta autem potestate atque auctoritate praedictae sint, manifestissime declaratur deum vere esse, qui homo factus salutaria praecepta hominibus tradidit. 3. Quid vero inde dicendum est quod prophetae de ipso antea praedixerant ‘non cessaturos principes ex luda neque duces ex femoribus eius, usquequo veniat ille, cui repositum este regnum scilicet, et "usquequo veniat expectatio gentium-? Manifestissime enim ex ipsa bistoria apparet et ex his, quae hodie pervidentur, quia ex temporibus Christi ultra reges apud ludaeos non extiterunt. Sed et omnes illae ambitiones Iudaicae, in quibus iactantiae quam plurimum gerebant et in quibus exultabant, id est vel de templi decore vel de altaris insignibus atque omnibus illis sacerdotalibus infulis indumentisque pontificum, simul universa destructa sunt. Completa est enim prophetia, quae dixerat: “Per dies multos sedebunt fili Israhel sine rege, sine principe; non erit hostia nec altare nec sacerdotium nec responsa”. His ergo testimonis utimur adversum eos, qui videntur adse rere de his, quae in Genesi ab lacob dicta sunt, quod de luda dieta sint et dicunt permanere adhue principem ex genere ludae, istum videlicet, qui est gentis ipsorum princeps, quem nominant patriarcham, nec deficere posse de semine eius qui permaneant usque ad adventum eius Christi, quem sibi ipsi describunt. Sed si verum est quod ait propheta, quia “dies multos sedebunt fili Israhel sine rege, sine principe; nec erit hostia nec altare nec sacerdotium”, et utique ex quo subversum est templum -nec hostiae- offeruntur “nec altare- invenitur “nec sacerdotiumconstat: certissimum est defecisse “principes ex luda-, sieut scriptum est, et -ducem ex femoribus eius, usquequo venit ille, eui repositum est Constat ergo quia ‘venit ille, cui repositum este, in quo et ‘expectatio gentium- est. Quod manifeste videtur impletum de multitudine eorum, qui per Christum deo ex diversis gentibus crediderunt. 4. Sed et in Deuteronomii cantico per prophetiam designatur pro peccatis prioris populi futura esse insensatae gentis electio, non alia utique quam haec, quae per Christum facta est. Sie enim ait: “Exacerbaverunt me in simulacris suis, et ego in zelo concitabo eos, in gente insipiente inritabo eos”. Est ergo satis evidenter agnoscere, quemammodum Hebraei, qui deum ‘exacerbasse’ dieuntur in his, qui non sunt du, et inritasse eum ‘in simulacris suis. inritati sunt et ipsi in zelotypia per ‘gentem insipientem”, quam deus -elegit- per adventum Christi lesu et discipulos eius. Sie enim dicit apostolus: “Videte enim vocationem vestram, fratres, quoniam non multi sapientes inter vos secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles; sed quae stulta sunt mundi elegit deus et ea, quae non sunt, ut ea, quae erant prius, destrueret”. Non ergo ‘glorietur- ‘carnalis Israhel-; ita namque ab apostolo vocatur: “non” inquam “glorietur caro in conspectu deic.
pass_a_gloss: But since human senses and common intellect are not sufficient for discussing such great and important things and, so to speak, visibly pronouncing on invisible things, we must also take up divine scripture testimonies for proof of what we say. Which testimonies, so that they may have certain and undoubted faith, either in what we are about to say or in what has already been said, it seems necessary first to show that the scriptures themselves are divine, that is, inspired by the Spirit of God. Therefore, we will briefly assign to this also from the divine scriptures themselves, which have moved us competently, producing, that is, from Moses, the first lawgiver of the Hebrew people, and from the words of Jesus Christ, the author and principle of the Christian religion and doctrine. For when many lawgivers have existed among Greeks and barbarians, and innumerable doctors or philosophers have promised to assert the truth, we do not recall any lawgiver who was able to instill a certain affection and study into the minds of foreign nations, so that they would either willingly receive his laws or defend them with all intention of their mind. No one, therefore, was able to insinuate and make the truth he saw not only into many other foreign nations but even into one nation, so that his knowledge or credulity would reach all. And indeed, it cannot be doubted that lawgivers have wished their laws to be observed by all people, if it could be done, and teachers, that the truth they saw would become known to all. But knowing that this was not possible at all, nor did such great virtue exist in them, which would also provoke foreign nations to observe their laws or assertions, they did not even dare to try or begin this, lest they be noted as imprudent and ineffective in this undertaking. But in the whole world, in all of Greece, and in all foreign nations, there are innumerable and immense people who, having abandoned their fathers' laws and the gods they thought were gods, have given themselves to the observance of Moses' law and the discipleship of Christ, and this not without great hatred having been stirred up against them by those who venerate idols, so that they are frequently afflicted with torments and sometimes even led to death; yet they embrace and guard the doctrine of Christ's word with all affection. And it is evident how the religion itself has grown in a short time, profiting from the punishments and deaths of its cultivators, and also from the plundering of goods and every kind of suffering tolerated by them; and it is all the more wonderful that not even the doctors themselves are sufficient or numerous enough: 'the word is preached' nonetheless 'in the whole world', so that 'Greeks and barbarians, wise and unwise' receive the religion of Christian doctrine. From which it is not doubtful that 'this is not done by human strength or resources', so that the word of Christ Jesus may grow strong with all power and credibility in the minds and souls of all. For it is evident that these things were predicted by him and confirmed by divine responses, when he says that 'you will be led before rulers and judges on account of me, as a testimony to them and to the nations'; and again: 'This gospel will be preached in all nations'; and again: 'Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name and cast out demons in your name? And I will say to them: Depart from me, workers of iniquity, for I never knew you.' If these things had been said by him but had not come to pass, perhaps they would seem less true and would not have any authority. But now, since the things that were predicted by him have come to pass with such great power and authority, it is most clearly declared that God truly exists, who, having become human, handed down salutary precepts to people. But what is to be said about the fact that the prophets predicted beforehand that 'the princes will not cease from Judah, nor the leaders from his thighs, until he comes to whom the kingdom has been entrusted, and until the expectation of the nations comes'? For it is most evident from history itself and from what is seen today that from the times of Christ, there have been no kings among the Jews. But also all those Jewish ambitions, in which they carried on much boasting and exultation, that is, either about the temple's decoration or the altar's insignia and all those priestly ornaments and pontifical garments, have been destroyed altogether. For the prophecy has been fulfilled, which said: 'The sons of Israel will sit for many days without a king, without a prince; there will be no sacrifice, no altar, no priesthood, no responses.' We use these testimonies against those who seem to assert that what was said by Jacob in Genesis about Judah remains to this day, namely, that a prince from the tribe of Judah, whom they call the patriarch, still endures, and that those who remain from his seed will not fail until the coming of Christ, whom they describe to themselves. But if it is true what the prophet says, that 'the sons of Israel will sit for many days without a king, without a prince; there will be no sacrifice, no altar, no priesthood', and indeed since the temple was overthrown, no sacrifices are offered, no altar is found, no priesthood exists, it is most certain that the princes from Judah have failed, as it is written, and the leader from his thighs, until he comes to whom the kingdom has been entrusted. It is therefore established that 'he has come to whom the kingdom has been entrusted', in whom also 'the expectation of the nations' is. Which is clearly seen to be fulfilled in the multitude of those who have believed in God through Christ from diverse nations. But also in the song of Deuteronomy, the election of a foolish nation is designated through prophecy as a future event, on account of the sins of the prior people, not another, indeed, than this one, which was made through Christ. For thus it says: 'They have provoked me with their idols, and I will provoke them with a foolish nation, I will irritate them with a stupid people.' It is therefore sufficiently evident to recognize how the Hebrews, who are said to have provoked God with those who are not gods and to have irritated him with their idols, have been irritated themselves in zealotry through the 'foolish nation', which God has chosen through the coming of Christ Jesus and his disciples. For thus the apostle says: 'See your calling, brothers, that not many wise men according to the flesh are among you, not many powerful men, not many noble men; but God has chosen the foolish things of the world and the things that are not, so that he may destroy the things that were.' Therefore, 'fleshly Israel' does not glory; for thus it is called by the apostle: 'not', I say, 'does flesh glory in the sight of God.'

pass_b_english: Since human senses and common understanding are not sufficient for discussing matters so great and weighty, nor for pronouncing visibly, as it were, on invisible things, we must also call upon the testimonies of divine Scripture to prove what we say. So that these testimonies may carry certain and undoubted authority both in what we are about to say and in what has already been said, it seems necessary first to show that the Scriptures themselves are divine — that is, inspired by the Spirit of God. Therefore we will briefly indicate this also from the divine Scriptures themselves, which have moved us convincingly — namely, from Moses, the first lawgiver of the Hebrew people, and from the words of Jesus Christ, the author and head of the Christian religion and doctrine.

Many lawgivers have arisen among Greeks and barbarians, and innumerable teachers and philosophers have claimed to proclaim the truth. Yet we recall no lawgiver who managed to instill in foreign nations any affection or zeal that would lead them either to receive his laws willingly or to defend them with all their heart. No one could so insinuate his perceived truth into even a single nation, let alone many, that knowledge or belief in it would reach everyone. And yet it cannot be doubted that lawgivers would have wished their laws to be observed by all people if it were possible, and teachers would have wished the truth they saw to be known to all. But knowing this was utterly impossible, and that no virtue of theirs was great enough to compel foreign nations to observe their laws or teachings, they did not even dare to try or begin, lest they be marked as imprudent for an ineffective and hopeless enterprise.

By contrast, in the whole world, in all Greece, and among all foreign nations, there are innumerable and vast multitudes who have abandoned their ancestral laws and the gods they once revered, and have given themselves to the observance of the law of Moses and the discipleship of Christ. They have done this despite the great hatred stirred up against them by those who venerate idols, so that they are frequently afflicted with torments and sometimes even put to death. Yet they embrace and guard the word of Christ's teaching with all their affection. It is evident how this religion has grown in a short time, advancing through the punishments and deaths of its adherents, and through the plundering of their goods and the endurance of every kind of suffering. And it is all the more remarkable that not even the teachers themselves are sufficiently numerous or qualified: yet 'the word is preached in the whole world' (Ps. 18:5 / Rom. 10:18), so that 'Greeks and barbarians, wise and unwise' (Rom. 1:14) receive the religion of Christian doctrine. From this there is no doubt that this is 'not by human strength or resources' (Ps. 43:4 / 44:3) that the word of Christ Jesus grows strong with all power and credibility in the minds and hearts of all.

For it is clear that these things were foretold by him and confirmed by divine responses. He said, 'You will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations' (Matt. 10:18). Again: 'This gospel will be preached in all nations' (Matt. 24:14). And again: 'Many will say to me on that day: Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name and cast out demons in your name? And I will say to them: Depart from me, you workers of iniquity, for I never knew you' (Matt. 7:22-23). If these things had been spoken by him but had not come to pass, they might seem less true and would lack authority. But now, since the things he foretold have come to pass with such great power and authority, it is most clearly declared that God truly exists — the One who, becoming human, handed down saving precepts to humanity.

What, then, must we say about the fact that the prophets foretold beforehand that 'the scepter shall not depart from Judah, nor the ruler's staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs, and to whom the expectation of the nations belongs' (Gen. 49:10)? It is most evident from history itself and from what is seen today that from the time of Christ onward there have been no kings among the Jews. Moreover, all those Jewish boasts — in which they took great pride and exultation, whether about the temple's splendor, the altar's insignia, or all the priestly ornaments and pontifical vestments — have been utterly destroyed. For the prophecy has been fulfilled: 'For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince, without sacrifice, without an altar, without priesthood, without an ephod' (Hos. 3:4). We cite these testimonies against those who claim that what Jacob said in Genesis about Judah still holds — that a prince from the tribe of Judah, whom they call the patriarch, still endures, and that his line will not fail until the coming of the Christ whom they expect. But if the prophet's word is true — that 'the children of Israel shall sit for many days without a king, without a prince; there shall be no sacrifice, no altar, no priesthood' (Hos. 3:4) — and indeed since the temple was overthrown no sacrifices are offered, no altar is found, no priesthood exists, then it is most certain that the princes of Judah have failed, as it is written, and the ruler from his loins, until he comes to whom the kingdom belongs. It is therefore established that 'he has come to whom the kingdom belongs, and in whom the expectation of the nations is' (Gen. 49:10). This is plainly seen fulfilled in the multitude of those who from diverse nations have believed in God through Christ.

Again, in the Song of Deuteronomy, the election of a foolish nation is foretold as a future consequence of the prior people's sins — and this is none other than the election accomplished through Christ. For it says: 'They provoked me with their idols; I will provoke them with a foolish nation, I will anger them with a stupid people' (Deut. 32:21). It is therefore sufficiently clear to recognize how the Hebrews, who are said to have provoked God with those who are not gods and to have angered him with their idols, have themselves been provoked to jealousy by the 'foolish nation' which God chose through the coming of Christ Jesus and his disciples. For the apostle says: 'Consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble; but God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise, God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong, God chose what is low and despised in the world, even things that are not, to bring to nothing things that are' (1 Cor. 1:26-28). Therefore 'fleshly Israel' has no ground for boasting; for as the apostle calls it: 'Let no flesh boast in the presence of God' (1 Cor. 1:29).

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances of the Latin. Pass B provides appropriate scripture citations (e.g., Matt 10:18, Gen 49:10, Hos 3:4, Deut 32:21, 1 Cor 1:26-28) which are required for the allusions present in the Latin. The title 'Divine Scripture Testimonies' correctly names the thought of the passage.
